title: Why Penalties Are Taking Over Football
topic: How the modern penalty has become football's most valuable and most disputed chance

sources_used.title: Why Premier League penalties are more valuable than ever

sections.voiceover: A tap-in looks certain. A penalty is statistically better. That gap is changing football. Look at the value of the reward and the question changes. A carefully built attack can end with a difficult finish, while a foul in the same area can create a nearly automatic shot from twelve yards. The issue is not that penalties exist. The issue is that the gap between a normal chance and a spot kick has become so large that players, coaches and referees are increasingly incentivised to chase the whistle.

Expected goals makes the imbalance easier to see. A tap-in can look certain on television and still be missed because the ball arrives at the wrong speed, a defender reaches the line, or the striker has one rushed touch. A penalty removes most of those variables. The kicker chooses the corner, the goalkeeper must wait for the strike, and the distance is fixed. That is why a penalty is commonly valued close to eight-tenths of a goal, while many open-play chances sit much lower. The exact number changes by model, but the practical lesson survives every model: winning a penalty can be more valuable than completing the attack that came before it.

Think about the difference between a one-on-one and a foul. A forward can beat the last defender, take a heavy touch and give the goalkeeper a chance. If the defender clips the same player a fraction earlier, the referee may award the most valuable restart in the sport. The attacking team does not receive the probability of the original chance; it receives a new chance with a higher baseline. That is why a harmless-looking collision can matter more than a brilliant piece of creation. The rule is consistent, but the reward can feel disconnected from the football that produced the incident.

The penalty was not born as a celebration of easy goals. It was a response to a problem in the early game: serious fouls near goal could go unpunished because the rules offered no proportionate remedy. William McCrum's proposal, adopted in the nineteenth century, created a defined location and a defined consequence. At first the idea was controversial. Some players even treated accepting a penalty as contrary to the spirit of a gentleman's game. The irony is that a rule created to protect attacking football now shapes attacking behaviour. A historical safeguard has become one of the sport's most strategically valuable weapons.

The modern game has widened the gap between ordinary chances and penalties. Better pitches, better boots and better analysis make it easier to reach the area. VAR then examines incidents that once disappeared inside the speed of a match. More reviews do not automatically mean more correct decisions; they mean more attention on the boundary between contact and foul play. At the same time, penalty taking has become a specialist craft. Teams train the run-up, the goalkeeper study, the preferred side and the delay before contact. The set piece is no longer an interruption. It is a prepared attacking phase with a very high expected return.

Cole Palmer's recent scoring numbers show why the debate becomes personal. A player can be genuinely outstanding in open play and still receive a large boost from a steady stream of penalties. The two facts can coexist. The problem begins when a goals total is used as if every goal carried the same difficulty. Four finishes in one match may contain a penalty, a rebound, a long-range strike and a created chance, yet the headline number compresses them into one statistic. Penalties do not make a player fraudulent. They do make simple goal totals less informative than they appear.

The same logic appears in the comparison between a penalty and a high-quality open-play chance. Even when a striker is clean through, the ball can be placed too close to the goalkeeper or the finish can be rushed. A penalty begins with the ball stationary and the goalkeeper constrained by the law. That does not remove pressure, and it does not guarantee a goal, but it changes the distribution of outcomes. The winning team receives a reward whose value is often higher than the chance that was interrupted. In analytical terms, the foul can be a better outcome than the attack itself.

Consider a wide attack that ends with a defender's late challenge. The original move may have produced a cross, a blocked shot or a pass back toward the edge of the box. Once the whistle goes, all of those possible outcomes disappear. The penalty replaces a branching sequence with one controlled attempt. That is why the best penalty analysis must compare the kick with the counterfactual: what would probably have happened if the foul had not been called? In many cases the answer is not a goal, or even a shot. It is continued possession. The punishment can therefore be dramatically larger than the lost opportunity.

VAR changed the atmosphere around the penalty area. The technology was introduced to correct obvious errors, but every review also changes what players believe is worth trying. A hand that once looked accidental can become a freeze-frame debate. A goalkeeper's movement can be measured down to a foot. A striker knows that a small touch may be re-examined from several angles. The result is a new kind of pressure: not just pressure on the referee, but pressure on the geometry of the incident. The slower the review becomes, the more the moment feels like a legal case rather than a football action.

Specialist takers expose another uncomfortable truth. The very best penalty takers can turn a high-value chance into a near routine. Harry Kane's record, and the consistency of other elite finishers, show how much technique can be built around a stationary ball. That is a compliment to the taker, not an insult. But it also means that a team with one specialist can convert a marginal foul into a reliable goal. The advantage is distributed unevenly: the defender makes one mistake, while the taker arrives with a rehearsed sequence designed to exploit the rules.

So what could change? One option is stricter officiating, reserving penalties for clear attempts to stop a shot or a decisive attacking action. Another is changing the goalkeeper's movement rules, although that risks creating a different technical problem. Moving the spot back would reduce conversion without removing the punishment, but it would also alter the history and feel of the game. None of these ideas is perfect. The most defensible starting point is narrower: distinguish a blatant denial of a scoring chance from contact that merely happens inside the box.

Brentford provide a useful case study because their success is not built on one famous superstar. Their attacking structure creates pressure, second balls and awkward decisions in the area. If a defender chooses the wrong moment, the reward is enormous. The club is not cheating by understanding that incentive. It is doing what any well-coached team should do: maximise the rules available to it. The uncomfortable conclusion is that the system encourages this behaviour. Blaming the players alone misses the design of the game that makes a soft foul more valuable than a patient possession.

The counterfactual matters most in incidents that look dramatic after the whistle. Imagine a forward receiving the ball near the corner of the area with defenders already recovering. Without the foul, the attack may produce a low-probability shot or a pass into a crowded lane. With the foul, the attacking side receives a set piece with a conversion rate close to ninety percent in some Premier League seasons. That is not a small correction. It is a jump from a fragile attack to an almost guaranteed scoring opportunity. The camera shows contact. The model shows how much the contact changed the game.

Penalty-winning numbers also distort how creative players are judged. A midfielder can carry the ball, draw a defender and win the kick, yet the assist belongs to nobody. Another player takes the shot and receives the goal. The same action can be described as intelligent attacking or as manufacturing a foul, depending on the viewer's sympathy. That ambiguity is why non-penalty goals and expected assists have become useful companion statistics. They do not tell the whole story. They simply separate different ways of contributing so that one scoreboard number does not decide the argument for us.

Plot the leading scorers on two axes: total goals and goals from open play. The shape of the graph changes immediately. Some players sit high because they finish chances created by the team. Others gain a larger share of their total from penalties. Neither profile is automatically superior. A penalty taker must still cope with pressure, scouting and the possibility of becoming the villain. But the graph makes a hidden assumption visible: treating every goal as an identical unit can overstate the similarity between very different attacking roles.

This is where the argument needs restraint. Players are not wrong to accept a penalty when a referee awards one. A club is not wrong to practise the set piece. And a goalkeeper is not wrong to use every legal advantage. The criticism belongs at the level of incentives. If the game rewards theatrical contact more than creative risk, behaviour will move toward theatrical contact. Fans can dislike the result without pretending the players invented the conditions. The question is not whether penalties are legitimate. It is whether the reward remains proportionate to the foul.

There is a setting where penalties feel completely right: the knockout shootout. The match has already exhausted open play. Every player knows that the next kick carries the weight of a season. The goalkeeper can become a hero, a substitute can create a legacy, and an unexpected taker can define a generation. In that context the penalty is not replacing an attack. It is testing nerve after the football has reached its limit. The same mechanism that feels artificial in a league match can feel dramatic and fair in a tournament conclusion.

Missed penalties explain why the kick remains human despite its statistical value. Roberto Baggio's 1994 World Cup final miss is remembered not because he lacked ability, but because the moment exposed the pressure that numbers cannot erase. A penalty is technically simple and emotionally enormous. That contradiction is part of its power. The argument is not that every kick should be made difficult. It is that the sport should decide when this particular kind of pressure is the appropriate consequence for an action.

In league football, the problem is accumulation. A season can contain hundreds of small decisions, each one turning a contested attack into a very high-value shot. Goals, corners and penalties begin to dominate the shape of matches, while the open-play work that created them becomes harder to remember. The game starts to resemble a sequence of rehearsed restarts. That is not because football has lost its skill. It is because the incentives increasingly favour the moments that pause the game.

Penalties are necessary. They protect attackers, punish clear offences and create some of football's most unforgettable scenes. But necessity is not the same as abundance. If a marginal touch can be worth more than a carefully built chance, the boundary has moved too far. The fairest correction is to let more attacks continue and reserve the biggest reward for the clearest denials. Keep the drama where it belongs: in moments that test footballers, not in every decision that happens to occur inside a rectangle.

hook: A tap-in looks certain. A penalty is statistically better. That gap is changing football.
ending: Penalties are necessary, but the reward should match the foul. Keep the drama, raise the threshold.
